metaDescription: Six cordless leaf vacuums at or under $300 from WORX, EGO and Greenworks, compared on metal impellers, mulch ratios, bag size and battery platforms.
expertTake: The WORX Trivac WG588 is the pick for anyone who wants a metal impeller, a stated 20:1 mulch ratio and a 40V platform with real parts support. The Greenworks 40V with a 5.0Ah pack in the box is the value choice for a complete kit. If you already own EGO batteries the LV5000 is excellent, but it is tool-only, so factor in the pack.
introParagraphs: At this level the interesting question stops being airflow and becomes what happens inside the housing. Metal impellers, published mulch ratios and larger bags are the details that separate a vacuum that lasts from one that clogs.
Cordless platforms dominate this band, so the battery you already own or plan to buy matters as much as the machine. Prices move, and the $300 cap reflects listing prices when this guide was updated.

products.name: WORX Trivac WG588 40V Cordless Leaf Vacuum Mulcher
products.description:
The WG588 is the machine that explains why impeller design matters. It uses triple-layer metal impellers rather than a plastic blade, and the listing states a 20:1 mulch ratio, which means twenty bags of leaves shrink toward one bag of mulch. Metal blades hold an edge longer and tolerate the occasional twig better than molded plastic, which is the usual failure point on cheaper vacuums.

Its 600 CFM and 100 MPH claims show a design aimed at volume over jet speed, which is the right balance for pulling leaves into the tube. Compared with the WG583 at 340 CFM and 210 MPH, it trades blowing speed for suction, and it also switches from blow to vacuum without tools.

Ownership centers on the 40V WORX battery family, so packs can be shared with other tools. Check whether the listing includes a pack and charger, since that changes the real cost. Empty the bag at half full, store the battery indoors and clear the impeller with the pack removed. It is the right choice for a homeowner who wants the vacuum to last. Expect the vacuum tube to feel long and slightly nose-heavy once the bag fills, so adjust the shoulder strap before you start. Keep the batteries on the charger overnight before a big weekend session, and swap them when the output drops rather than running them flat.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want a durable metal-impeller mulcher.
pros: Stated 20:1 mulch ratio cuts bag count
Toolless switch between blow and vacuum
cons: Low 100 MPH speed is weaker for pavement debris
Check whether battery and charger are included

products.name: Greenworks 40V Leaf Blower Vacuum 505 CFM 5.0Ah
products.description:
This Greenworks ships as a complete kit with a 5.0Ah pack and charger, so the box contains everything needed to start. Its brushless motor, variable speed dial and turbo button give it both control and a burst when needed, and the 505 CFM claim is in line with other 40V tools.

Compared with the WORX WG588, it lacks a published mulch ratio and a metal impeller claim, so it is the more conventional design, but a larger pack means a long first session. The turbo boost is useful for matted spots but drains the pack quickly.

Greenworks parts and packs are easy to find, and the same battery runs a wide tool family. Store the pack indoors and empty the bag regularly. It is the value choice for someone who does not already own a battery. A turbo button is best used in short bursts for matted corners, not for the entire job, because it empties the pack much faster than the dial. Wear eye protection when the nozzle is near gravel, since small stones can fly out at speed.
products.bestFor: First-time cordless buyers who need the battery included.
pros: Complete kit with a 5.0Ah pack and charger
Variable dial plus turbo for control
cons: No published mulch ratio or impeller material

products.name: EGO Power+ LV5000 Leaf Vacuum Mulcher 500 CFM

specList.label: Included
specList.value: Tool only, no battery or charger

products.description:
The LV5000 uses a six-blade metal impeller with a stated 16:1 mulch ratio and a 40 liter bag that is easy to empty. Blower mode claims up to 500 CFM and up to 210 MPH with the tapered nozzle fitted, so it covers both jobs well. Metal blades and a large bag are the two features owners value most in a leaf vacuum.

The catch is that the listing is for the tool only. Without an EGO battery and charger you cannot use it, and the pack is the most expensive part of the system. If you already own an EGO mower or trimmer, this is an excellent add-on; if not, price the full setup.

EGO service and parts are widely available. Store packs indoors and clear the impeller with the pack removed. It is for owners already invested in the 56V platform. Plan the full cost before buying: the tool is only part of the spend, and a battery plus charger can equal the tool's price again. If you already own the platform, it is a very strong purchase, and spare packs from your other tools will keep it running all afternoon.
products.bestFor: Existing EGO owners who need a bare tool.
pros: Six-blade metal impeller with 16:1 mulch ratio
High air speed with the tapered nozzle
cons: 56V pack adds cost if you do not own one

products.name: WORX WG583 40V Cordless Leaf Blower Vacuum Mulcher
products.description:
The WG583 flips the balance of its sibling: 340 CFM and 210 MPH with a 12:1 mulch ratio. That makes it a blower-first machine that also vacuums, better at lifting debris off hard surfaces than moving big leaf piles.

Dual-speed control keeps things simple, and brushless power helps run time. It shares the 40V WORX platform with the WG588, so packs interchange.

If you mostly blow and occasionally vacuum, it is the more efficient purchase. If you mulch heavily, the WG588's higher ratio is better. Its higher airflow volume suits blowing leaves into a bed edge or a pile for collection. Use it as the blower for the first pass, then switch to vacuum mode in the corners where a pile would be hard to manage. Rinse nothing; wipe it down with a dry cloth.
cons: Lower mulch ratio than the WG588
Less volume for big leaf piles

products.name: Greenworks 48V 520 CFM Leaf Vacuum 2 x 4.0Ah
products.description:
This Greenworks uses two 24V packs to make 48V, which supports higher power than a single 40V pack. The listing claims 520 CFM and 240 MPH, a strong blend of volume and speed.

It is the choice here if you want the highest voltage and a complete kit with two packs, at the cost of carrying two batteries.

Store packs indoors and clear the impeller with packs removed. The two-pack arrangement means you get a built-in spare, but you must keep both fully charged and rotate them evenly. Label the packs with tape so you remember which one went into the tool last, and store them together so their ages match. This evens out capacity loss over several seasons and avoids one pack failing early.
products.bestFor: Higher voltage and a complete two-pack kit.

products.name: MZK 40V Brushless Leaf Vacuum Mulcher 700 CFM
products.description:
The MZK is the lowest cost route to a large bag and a big airflow claim. A brushless 40V motor, a 40 liter bag and an anti-jam design make it attractive on paper.

The tradeoff is the brand: no published mulch ratio or impeller material, and support is thin.

It suits a buyer who prioritizes capacity over certainty. Because the brand is newer, register the product if the maker offers it and keep every receipt and packaging label. Photograph the serial number. Replacement bags and impellers should be confirmed available before you buy, since an unsupported wear part can retire the whole machine. Treat the big airflow number as a hopeful maximum.
pros: Highest airflow claim of the group

buyingCriteria.explanation: The WORX WG588 uses triple-layer metal impellers and the EGO LV5000 a six-blade metal impeller, while cheaper vacuums use molded plastic. Metal holds up against twigs and acorns and keeps its edge. If you shred a lot of leaves each fall, this is the single most durable feature to look for. Look at whether the impeller can be reached and replaced without special tools, since a wear item that cannot be changed turns into landfill.

The WG588 states 20:1, the LV5000 16:1 and the WG583 12:1. A higher ratio means fewer bags to carry out and faster compost. Use it to compare tools within the same maker, and note that wet leaves give a lower real ratio. If you compost, a better ratio pays off every autumn, but only if the leaves are dry when they go in.

The EGO LV5000 is tool-only, while the Greenworks 40V ships with a 5.0Ah pack. A pack and charger can cost as much as the tool, so compare complete setups. Total the tool, pack and charger on the same page before you compare two listings, or a cheap tool-only deal will mislead you.

A 40 liter bag on the EGO and MZK cuts stops. Look for a bag that opens fully and does not need a zipper wrestle. Large bags are heavy when full, so a lighter, smaller bag you empty often can be easier on your back.

The WG588 favors 600 CFM at 100 MPH for vacuuming, the WG583 favors 210 MPH at 340 CFM for blowing. Choose by whether you blow or vacuum more. If you use the machine mostly as a blower, favor speed, because suction matters only when the vacuum tube is on.

WORX 40V, Greenworks 40V and EGO 56V all share packs with other tools. A standalone brand cannot. Think about where you will find a replacement pack in year three. Reusing a battery across tools lowers your cost per tool, which is a better measure of value than the sticker price of one machine.

specDecoder.meaning: How much volume leaves shrink to. 20:1 means twenty parts of leaves become one part of mulch. It changes what you should expect from a spring cleanup versus an autumn one.
specDecoder.watchFor: The WG588 states 20:1 versus the WG583's 12:1; wet leaves give lower real ratios.

specDecoder.meaning: The blades that shred leaves. Metal outlasts plastic. This is the part most likely to wear out first.
specDecoder.watchFor: The EGO and WG588 state metal; others do not.

specDecoder.meaning: Claimed air volume for suction. Use it to rank tools that do the same job rather than to predict real output.
specDecoder.watchFor: The MZK claims 700 CFM and the WG588 600; brand methods differ.

specDecoder.meaning: Claimed air speed for blowing. Pair it with CFM so you do not buy a fast, thin stream when you wanted suction.
specDecoder.watchFor: The WG583 claims 210 MPH versus the WG588's 100.

specDecoder.meaning: Two packs combined for higher voltage, such as 2 x 24V for 48V. Always confirm that both packs ship with the kit.
specDecoder.watchFor: Both packs must be installed to run the Greenworks 48V.

howWeEvaluated.title: Impeller design
howWeEvaluated.description: We graded metal impellers and stated mulch ratios highest. The WG588 at 20:1 and the LV5000 at 16:1 led. Unstated designs scored lower. That makes the impeller the first thing we checked, since it is both the most visible durability feature and the most common failure.

howWeEvaluated.title: Kit completeness
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked whether battery and charger ship in the box. The Greenworks 40V with a 5.0Ah pack scored higher than the tool-only LV5000. Where a listing was silent on the box contents, we flagged the uncertainty rather than assume a battery was included.

howWeEvaluated.title: Airflow balance
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared volume and speed claims for the vacuum job. A high CFM matters more for suction than MPH. We also noted that claimed airflow is measured differently by every maker, so we weighted design details more than the single number.

howWeEvaluated.title: Platform value
howWeEvaluated.description: We counted how many other tools share each pack. WORX, Greenworks and EGO scored well. Parts availability and a clear warranty counted for as much as raw claimed performance.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered bag design, parts and warranty. Owner feedback patterns on impeller wear informed durability. Owner feedback patterns on jamming and bag zippers shaped the handling score.

cards.text: A high mulch ratio and a metal impeller. Finely shredded leaves break down far faster than whole ones.

maintenance.task: Remove the pack before clearing jams
maintenance.why: Accidental start with hands near the impeller is a serious injury risk. Take the pack off before any inspection, and leave it off until the housing is closed.
A full bag cuts suction and adds weight. Compressed air clears vents better than a wet rag.
Lithium cells age faster when stored full or empty.
Nicks and bends reduce shredding and cause imbalance.
Dust blocks cooling slots and heats the motor.

faq.q: What does mulch ratio really tell me?
faq.a: It is the volume reduction of leaves. A 20:1 claim means far fewer bags, but wet leaves reduce the real ratio. Match the choice to how much you shred, not to the biggest number.
For heavy use, yes. Metal resists twigs and keeps its edge. Plastic is fine for light, dry leaves. Note that a stronger impeller is the main reason to pay more in this band.

faq.q: Is the EGO LV5000 a good deal if I have no EGO battery?
faq.a: Price the full setup first. The pack and charger can cost as much as the tool. Check the box contents first, because one pick here is tool-only.

faq.q: Why does the Greenworks 48V use two packs?
faq.a: Two 24V packs in series make 48V, giving higher power with smaller, lighter packs. Series packs mean the tool will not run with just one installed.
Poorly. Wet leaves clog the impeller and lower the mulch ratio. Let them dry.
